candidates.title: Certain About Clouds
candidates.pitch: A bureaucratic inspection machine looks at cloud-like blots (procedural, or painted by the visitor) and announces what they are with 99-percent-plus certainty: a lighthouse, a nomad, a parade float. Its reasoning transcript is delightfully wrong but fully deterministic, so the visitor can learn its rulebook by predicting its verdicts before it speaks, then try to build a blot that forces it to say a chosen word. The fun is the moment you can finish its sentence.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless. Confident machine verdicts are a permanent cultural joke, and this one swaps randomness for a rulebook that rewards understanding.

research.summary: Pareidolia (seeing faces or objects in random patterns) and its umbrella term apophenia give the machine's one big delusion. Classic expert systems (rule base, inference engine, explanation facility that replays which rules fired) give the structure: a forward-chaining rulebook with a printed reasoning trace is both historically real and ideal for a learnable joke. Research on model calibration (stated confidence versus real accuracy) gives the comic law: this machine's certainty is a fixed function that ignores contradicting evidence. Existing confidently-wrong chatbot parodies appear to rely on a language model and randomness; a deterministic, learnable machine is a different experience.

facts.claim: Pareidolia is the tendency to perceive faces or familiar shapes in random or ambiguous patterns (seen in search results 2026-10-12).
Published machine-learning research (for example a 2017 paper on modern neural networks) studies the gap between a classifier's stated confidence and its real accuracy.

Apophenia is the tendency to find patterns in unrelated data, and pareidolia counts as one kind; as of 2026-10-12, per a mental-health education site and a psychology site (blended search summary, unconfirmed).

A textbook expert system has a rule base, an inference engine that matches and fires rules, and an explanation facility that lists the rules fired; as of 2026-10-12, per a university course page (unconfirmed).
Small satirical sites that give confidently wrong answers already exist, as of 2026-10-12, per two product directory listings (unconfirmed).

inspirations: classic rule-based expert systems and their why/how traces
satirical confidently-wrong chatbots (as a contrast, not a copy)

design.coreLoop: Each case is a 48x48 blot with six measured features (tallness, symmetry, holes, jaggedness, blob count, density). The visitor predicts the verdict word and a confidence band, then the machine stamps its verdict and prints a numbered reasoning trace of the rules that fired. A rule notebook lets the visitor state a hypothesis (feature, threshold, label) and see it scored against every past case. Depth comes from rule priority quirks (first high-salience rule wins, contradicting evidence is ignored, confidence rises with the number of agreeing weak rules). Later audits unlock a build-a-blot mode where the goal is to force a target word, for example the machine's word for a wandering traveller.
sophisticationHooks: Real forward-chaining engine in about 30 rules with salience and conflict resolution, plus an explanation trace that replays the firing order
Hypothesis notebook that auto-tests the visitor's own rule against all seen cases and highlights the counterexamples
Deterministic seeded blot generator plus freehand painting with pointer events, features computed live
Shareable URL hash that stores a case seed and the visitor's rule list, plus a printable certificate of certainty as a screenshot moment
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: blot generator and painter, feature extractor, rule engine with about 30 rules and 40 verdict words (lighthouse, nomad, jubilee float and similar), predict-then-reveal loop, rule notebook, build-a-blot target mode with 6 audits, light and dark, keyboard and touch, about panel. Cut: sound, accounts, any online data, user-written rule languages beyond the single-condition notebook.
risks: Rule base must be learnable: ship a script-checked simple decision tree that reproduces at least 90 percent of verdicts, and test with fresh eyes.
Could drift into random-feeling output if salience ties are not resolved deterministically; fix with a stable tie-break order shown in the trace.
Expert-system and calibration claims are partly unconfirmed; the about panel should list only verified sources and show the rest as 'as of 2026-10-12, per <source>'.
Must parody a generic automated certainty, never a real product's voice or branding; use an invented bureau name and hand-drawn stamps.

candidates.title: The Nickname Oracle
candidates.pitch: A pompous hockey prediction machine picks a winner for any two of the 32 league nicknames using one absurd theory: the nicknames form a hidden ecology (predators beat prey, weather beats machinery, myths beat everything but have a weakness). The visitor tries to call its pick before it announces it, learns the hidden type chart through its smug explanations, then runs a full machine-made 32-team season table and screenshots the result.
candidates.whyNow: The new league season is under way (as of 2026-10-12, per NHL.com, unconfirmed), which is when fans want to argue forecasts; the page stays playable for the whole season and beyond.

research.summary: Team nicknames in the league come from very mixed origins (animals, mythology, weather and terrain, trades, local history), and several outlets publish origin-story roundups, which is the raw material for a nickname-only theory with no real results, players or odds involved. The league season runs on a long schedule that started in late September 2026 (reported, unconfirmed), so a fan toy about forecasting is topical. The machine's tone parodies automated, overconfident punditry in general; its internal logic (a nickname type chart, tie-breakers on word shape, a fixed overconfidence law) is what makes it learnable. Shared idea with the confident-machine genre: certainty that is consistent, not random.

inspirations: elemental type charts in monster-collecting games

design.coreLoop: The page shows two nicknames. The visitor picks who the Oracle will back and how sure it will sound, then the Oracle announces its pick with a grandly wrong explanation citing its theory (type advantage, word-shape tie-breakers, and a fixed overconfidence law). A streak counter and a discovery log fill in the hidden type chart as the visitor makes correct calls. Mastery unlocks the season mode, where the visitor predicts the Oracle's whole 32-team table, scored by distance, and a share link encodes the visitor's chart guesses.
sophisticationHooks: Hidden type chart over about 8 nickname classes plus three deterministic tie-breakers (vowel count, word length, alphabetical order) that the visitor can discover
Explanation generator that assembles bureaucratic pundit sentences from the rules that fired, so each verdict teaches something
Season mode: round-robin table computed by the same rules, with predict-the-table scoring and a shareable URL hash
Discovery log and a 'break the Oracle' challenge that asks for a matchup where its confidence drops below its usual level (only one rule does this)
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: 32-nickname table with class assignments hand-made by us, rule engine, explanation generator, predict-the-pick game with streaks, discovery log, season table mode, share hash, light and dark, keyboard and touch, about panel with a clear 'nonsense, not a forecast, not betting advice' label. Cut: real schedules or results, standings feeds, player names, logos, any odds display, audio.
risks: Season-start and 84-game claims are unconfirmed; the page should avoid depending on them or show them as 'as of 2026-10-12, per NHL.com'.
The roster of 32 nicknames must be checked against the current league before build (a recent franchise rename is possible and not verified here); keep the list in one data file.
Must be unmistakably a joke with no betting or odds framing: no real results, no player names, no logos, plain-text nicknames only, an unofficial-fan-parody label.
Competes with other hockey puzzles in the pool; the differentiator is a learnable fictional theory, not stats.
